questions.enonce_markdown:
Distinguish between the following terms:

(i) Allometric and isometric growth

(ii) Growth and development. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Allometric and isometric growth** *(4 marks)*

| Isometric growth | Allometric growth |
|---|---|
| **All parts of the organism grow at the same rate** as the whole body | **Different parts grow at different rates** |
| The **proportions of the body stay the same** as it gets bigger | The **proportions of the body change** during growth |
| Examples: **fish**, and the larval stages of some insects | Examples: **humans** (the head is about one quarter of body length at birth but about one eighth in the adult; the legs grow proportionally more); the large claw of the male fiddler crab |
| A plot of the log of an organ's size against the log of the body size has a **slope of 1** | The slope of the log-log plot is **different from 1** |

**(ii) Growth and development** *(4 marks)*

| Growth | Development |
|---|---|
| A **permanent, irreversible increase in size (and dry mass)** of an organism, brought about by **cell division and cell enlargement** | The **series of changes in form and complexity** from the zygote to the mature organism, involving **cell differentiation and morphogenesis** |
| **Quantitative**: it can be **measured** (height, mass, number of cells) | **Qualitative**: it is a change in structure and function and cannot easily be measured |
| Example: increase in the height of a seedling | Example: a tadpole changing into a frog, a seed becoming a flowering plant |

The two normally occur together, but they are different: a cell can differentiate (develop) without an increase in size.

questions.enonce_markdown: Differentiate between growth in flowering plants and growth in mammals. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Growth in flowering plants | Growth in mammals |
|---|---|
| **Continues throughout life** (**indeterminate** growth) | Usually **stops at maturity** (**determinate** growth) |
| **Localised in regions of cell division** (**meristems**: apical meristems for length, **cambium** for girth) | Occurs **all over the body**, in all the tissues |
| Cells **enlarge a lot by taking in water** into large **vacuoles**, which gives most of the increase in size | Increase in size comes mainly from **cell division and the synthesis of new cytoplasm**; cells do not enlarge much |
| Controlled by **plant growth substances** (**auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins**) | Controlled by **hormones** (**growth hormone, thyroxine, sex hormones, insulin**) |
| Gives **primary growth** (length) and **secondary growth** (increase in girth, annual rings) | **No secondary growth**; some organs (brain) stop growing early, and there are **growth spurts** (infancy, puberty) |
| Strongly **influenced by the environment** (light, gravity, water, temperature, tropisms) | Less directly influenced by the environment (diet is important) |
| Some organs (leaves, flowers, fruits) have **limited growth** | Growth of organs is **coordinated**, giving a fixed adult shape |

questions.enonce_markdown: Outline the role of auxins in the development of plants. *[6 marks]* *(4, 4, 6, 6 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Auxins** (mainly **indoleacetic acid, IAA**) are made in the **shoot tip (apical meristem), young leaves and developing seeds** and move down the plant. Their roles:

1. **Cell elongation.** Auxin makes the cell wall more plastic (it stimulates proton pumping into the wall, which loosens the cellulose cross-links), so the cells **take up water and elongate**; this causes **growth in length of shoots**.
2. **Phototropism and geotropism.** Auxin is redistributed to the **shaded side** of a shoot, where it increases cell elongation, so the shoot **bends towards the light**. In a horizontal root and shoot, auxin collects on the lower side: it **stimulates elongation in the shoot** (it bends up) but **inhibits elongation in the root** (it bends down).
3. **Apical dominance.** Auxin from the apical bud **inhibits the growth of the lateral (axillary) buds**; if the tip is cut off, the side buds grow and the plant becomes bushy.
4. **Root development.** Auxin stimulates the formation of **adventitious roots** from cuttings (rooting powder) and the growth of lateral roots.
5. **Fruit development.** Auxin from the pollinated flower and seeds stimulates the **growth of the ovary into the fruit**; it can produce **seedless (parthenocarpic) fruits** and prevents early **fruit and leaf fall** (abscission).
6. **Differentiation of vascular tissues** (xylem and phloem), and stimulation of **cambium** activity. At high concentration, synthetic auxins such as **2,4-D** are used as **selective weedkillers**.

*Any six well-explained points gain full marks.*
